zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Review aid (not transcribed): The supplied page subset of Entry Words Data of Nippojisho was consulted after an independent scan reading for lexical identification and coverage. NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The returned transcription choices and English line notes are this reviewer’s scan-based work, not a copied NINJAL transcription.

lines.note: The opening continues the preceding definition of a month-long office. Nenguiǒji introduces the corresponding annual office; the worn n is read with the year-long gloss below. The visible Of- begins officio and is not a long-s form.

runs.text: ficio que dura por hum anno. ¶

lines.note: Ficio completes officio: an appointment lasting a year. Sumǒno begins the example concerning the official who supervises wrestling; the caron is retained.

runs.text: guiǒjini tatçu, l, ſumǒno guiǒjiuo ſuru.

lines.note: The alternatives mean serving as a sumo referee or performing that office. The printed l is the Latin alternative marker, not part of the Japanese phrase.

runs.text: Ter officio de ajuntar, & fazer trauar os

lines.note: The Portuguese explains the office as bringing the wrestlers together and having them engage. Trauar is the historical spelling and should not be modernized.
Lutadores completes the object of the preceding verbs. The comparison with padrinhos da luta describes the referee’s mediating or supervisory role.
Guiǒji, zuru, ita gives the forms of the verb meaning to carry out religious practice. The Portuguese starts a definition in terms of performing works, continued below.
De penitencia specifies the works as penitential exercises. This short continuation belongs to the verb, not the fisherman entry that follows.
Guiojin is explained by sunadoru fito, a person who fishes, and directly glossed Peſcador. Abrasion weakens several strokes in the Japanese synonym without supporting a different word.
Guioju, literally fish gathering, denotes a shoal of fish. The initial is G, not OCR C; pei- is the printed beginning of peixes across the physical break.
The example says that a shoal of fish goes upstream against the current. The repeated Guioju clarifies the headword; the OCR Gutoju misread the short i.

runs.text: O cardume de peixe ſobe contra a corrente.

lines.note: This is the Portuguese translation of the upstream-swimming example. Peixe has a visible x, not the OCR c. Final S. is an upright written-register label, outside the italic translation.

Guiǒjut is a religious rite or practice, explained by voconǒ nori and by prayers and ceremonies. The final headword letter is t, not OCR r; the Sino-Japanese checked ending is retained rather than expanded.
Monias completes ceremonias. Guiǒjutuo tçucuſu means carrying out these rites fully; the damaged opening is supported by the headword and surviving types, not the garbled OCR Ganǒjutuo.
The translation continues with performing these prayers and ceremonies. The printed deprecaçoẽs is preserved with its historical nasal notation rather than normalized.
Todas as forças and efficacia complete the instruction to perform the rites with all one’s strength and effectiveness. The first vowel of todas corrects OCR tadas.
Guiomocu is explicitly explained as the eyes of a fish. Vt, is italic and introduces the comparison on the following row; it is not part of the Japanese headword.

Guiomocuuo totte xuguiocuni fiſu means taking fish eyes and comparing them with precious jewels. The f in fiſu belongs to the Japanese verb for comparison; Cõpa- begins the Portuguese infinitive on the next line.

runs.text: rar os olhos do peixe a pedras precioſas.

lines.note: Rar completes Cõpa-rar, and the translation explicitly compares fish eyes to precious stones. The final upright S. marks written usage rather than belonging to the italic sentence.
Guiôna is illustrated with a person who magnifies or exaggerates things. The clear G corrects OCR C, and the circumflex must not be assimilated to neighboring caroned headwords.
Carecedor completes encarecedor. Guiôna coto supplies a second example, now applying the adjective to a thing rather than a person.
The second example is translated as something great and extraordinary. This short line closes Guiôna and is separate from the religious practitioner below.

runs.text: Guiǒnin. Voconǒ fito. i, Guiǒtaiuo ſuru

lines.note: Guiǒnin is a person who performs religious practice, further explained as someone who undertakes guiǒtai. Voconǒ fito and the longer paraphrase describe the same practitioner.

runs.text: Homem penitente, ou que faz obras,

lines.note: Fito completes the Japanese paraphrase. The Portuguese calls this person penitential or one who performs works, whose description continues below.
Exercises of virtue completes the description of Guiǒnin. The phrase is a continuation of the person’s practices, not a new headword.
Guionicu pairs fish with flesh or meat, matching Vuo, xiximura and the two Portuguese nouns. The visible separator after Vuo is a comma rather than the draft’s full stop.
Guioqei is an honorific expression of joy or congratulation, paraphrased Von yorocobi. Several abraded headword strokes produced OCR Giioqei; the repeated example below supplies a local comparator.

runs.text: ſe dão as boas feſtas, perabens, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The expression is used for greetings on festive occasions and congratulations. Perabens retains the printed historical vowel, while italic Vt, introduces the example below.
Guioqei medetai gives the congratulatory formula. The scan shows the same headword as above, not OCR Curioqei; this short Japanese example remains a separate physical row.
Guioqen is an honorific sword, paraphrased Votçurugui and exemplified by the king’s sword. The initial sequence is Guio-, not the OCR Gaio-.
The definition also includes the sword of a great lord. The damaged vowel in dalgum is compatible with u, completing the ordinary contracted Portuguese expression rather than OCR dalgam.
Guiôqi is explained as the end of the world, Yono ſuye. The headword’s visible circumflex is retained even though the following example has a differently directed mark.
Youa guiǒqini voyobu says that the world reaches its final period. The example’s caron is not regularized to the headword’s circumflex; the Portuguese begins describing a world nearing its end.
Acabando and enpejorando complete the explanation: the world is ending and worsening. The historical spelling with n before p remains unchanged.
Guioqua is the fire used in fishing, literally sunadori no fi. Both the G of the headword and u of Sunadorinofi correct OCR confusions; the visible joined spelling of the paraphrase is retained.
Cão completes pes-cão, explaining that fishermen use this fire at night. The broken word is preserved across its two physical rows.
Guiôraxij first describes something great; the example uses the adverbial Guiôraxù. The printed grave over the final u is distinct from the circumflex over o.
With the preceding adverb, monouo yǔ fito means a person who speaks exaggeratedly about things. The worn t in fito is recoverable from the remaining ink and the person-centered translation.
Muito as couſas completes the description of someone who exaggerates things greatly. It is the end of the example, not a detached lexical entry.
Guioren denotes an honorific hanging blind, paraphrased Von ſudare and Miſu. The Portuguese calls these mats or screens; the worn Guio- is not OCR Caio-.

runs.text: dependurão nas portas, ou janellas de peſſoas

lines.note: The blinds are hung in doors or windows belonging to people whose status is specified on the next row. Dependurão and janellas retain their printed spellings.
Nobres completes the preceding definition: these blinds are associated with noble people. The word remains a distinct body row even though it is very short.
Guioreo denotes silk of yamabuki color. The unaccented final reo is retained and is distinct from the accented fishing term on the next entry; OCR Cutoreo is not supported.

runs.text: ſeda de cor de hũas certas fulas amarelas.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains the silk’s color by comparison with certain yellow flowers. The unusual printed fulas is retained as visible rather than replaced with modern flores.
Guioreô, explained by Sunadorino cari, is fishing. This headword has the visible circumflex lacking in Guioreo above, and the Portuguese Peſcaria confirms a different entry.
Guiorin gives fish and scales in its literal paraphrase, then explicitly equates the term with Vuo, fish. The double z in vrocuzzu is retained rather than normalized to a modern spelling.
Guiǒriqi is the power of religious practice, Voconǒ chicara. The worn caroned o remains part of a single headword; Força has a cedilla, and peni- continues below.
Tencia completes penitencia; the rest adds other virtuous exercises. The scan supports outros exercicios virtuoſos rather than the draft’s garbled sequence.
Guiorui denotes a kind or category of fish, explained by Vuono tagui. The Portuguese deliberately gives both species and genus as descriptive alternatives.
De peixe completes the classification gloss. This is a real short continuation, not furniture or a separate entry.
Guiôſan is praising or extolling, literally Fome auogu. The Portuguese engrã- abbreviates the nasal consonant and continues onto the next row.
Decer completes engrã-decer. Guiôſanni yǔ introduces speaking in exaggerated praise, with the Portuguese dema- continued below.
Siadamente completes demasiadamente: praising or magnifying things excessively. The long-s opening follows the printed division rather than a new word.
Guiôſanna is the adjectival expression for something great and extraordinary. The doubled n is visible and distinguishes the form from a bare noun.
Guiôſanni is the corresponding adverbial form, glossed as greatly or with magnifying praise. It is a separate headword from the preceding -na form.
Guioſat, paraphrased Von fumi, is an honorific term for a letter. The final t is the printed checked ending, not a defective modernized syllable.
Reſpeito completes the explanation that this term for a letter is used respectfully. The short row belongs to Guioſat.
Guiǒſǒ concerns appearance or facial expression. Both Catachi tokens are printed and retained; the Portuguese describes the figure or countenance of a living person.
The gloss specifies a living person, then begins the example Guiǒſǒmini-/cuxi. The adjective is divided without a visible terminal hyphen after mini, so none is supplied.

runs.text: Estar o roſto, ou home des figurado.

lines.note: Cuxi completes the adjective describing an unpleasant or disfigured appearance. The Portuguese explains this as a disfigured face or person. The scan leaves home without a secure final m or tilde; that printed form and the locally spaced des figurado are retained rather than normalized.
Guioſon is a fishing settlement, explained by Sunadorino zaixo. The terminal pes- belongs to the Portuguese pescadores on the next physical row.
Cadores completes pes-cadores, closing the definition of a fishermen’s settlement. It is not a separate headword.
Guioſui combines fish and water in its Japanese explanation. The Portuguese first says fish-water and then clarifies the relation in the continuation.
The clarification is water in which fish swim. This avoids interpreting the preceding phrase as water extracted from a fish.
Guiǒtai is penitential practice. Guiǒtaiuo tçu- begins an example meaning to carry out such practices fully; the hyphen is visible at the column edge.
Cuſu completes tçu-cuſu, to carry out fully. The translation describes great penances and begins the reference to other good exercises, divided as ou-/tros.
Tros completes outros, adding other good practices to penitence. This short continuation closes the entry before the different sense of obstruction.

Guiôtai is explained by todocôru coto, being delayed or impeded. The initial G corrects OCR C. Only one arm of the headword’s vowel mark is strong; the draft’s circumflex is retained as the usable reading, with the graphic damage noted rather than silently turning it into a grave.
The Portuguese completes the sense of something being hindered or obstructed. The upright S. is a written-register label, while algũa retains the mark on u.
Guiotan, literally a fish’s qimo, is here explicitly fish bile or gall. The short i in the headword corrects OCR Gutotan, and Vt, introduces the bitter-taste example.
The example says that fish gall is exceedingly bitter. S. labels the Japanese example as written usage; the following italic O begins its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: fel do peixe he ſummamente amargoſo.

lines.note: Completes the translation: fish gall is supremely bitter. The historical amargoſo is retained instead of modern amargo.
Guiǒten combines looking up to heaven with Vodoroqu, being astonished. The worn Guio- and the caron are read with the repeated example below; Es- starts the Portuguese espanto.
Panto completes espanto, and Guiǒtenſuru means becoming astonished. The visible n before ſuru corrects OCR u without introducing an unprinted word boundary.
Guioteqi is the flute of a fisherman, Sunadorino fuye. Frauta is the printed Portuguese form; it is not modernized to flauta.
Cador completes pes-cador, identifying the flute’s owner or user. The short line remains in the body.

Guiotǒ is a fish-cutting blade, explained by Vuono catana. The Portuguese offers cutelo or faca. Only the rising arm of the caron is strong; no period is visible in the clear gap after the headword, so the draft’s period has been removed.
Cortar peixe specifies the blade’s function: cutting fish. It completes the preceding knife definition.
Guiotô means a fish’s head, exactly matched by Vuono atama and Cabeça de peixe. This is separate from the knife and fishing-light homophones around it.
Guiotô here means a fisherman’s light or fire, paraphrased with Sunadori and tomoxibi. The initial sequence is Guio-, not OCR Guro-.

runs.text: que peſcão de noite os peſcadores.

lines.note: The fire is used by fishermen fishing at night. This repeats the functional explanation given earlier for Guioqua without merging the entries.
Guiǒtocu denotes the benefit or merit of religious practice, Voconǒ tocu. Mere- begins merecimento across the physical line break.

runs.text: cimento de virtude, ou obras de penitencia.

lines.note: Cimento completes merecimento, linking merit with virtue and penitential works. The Portuguese noun is virtude, not OCR virtide.

runs.text: Guiouô. Sunadorino voqina. i, Toxi yot-

lines.note: Guiouô is an elderly or experienced fisherman, first paraphrased Sunadorino voqina. Toxi yot- starts a second description whose past-tense form ends on the next line.

runs.text: Peſcador velho, ou que ha mui-

lines.note: Ta completes yot-ta, and guiojin is visibly separated as the fisherman noun. The phrase means an aged fisherman; the translation also allows long experience in the trade. OCR tagurojin concealed both the boundary and the i.
To completes mui-to: someone who has practiced the occupation for a long time. This is the experienced-fisherman alternative, not a further age definition.
Guioxen, paraphrased Sunadorino fune, denotes a fishing vessel. The final adjective describing that vessel appears on the next row.
Peſcareza completes the fishing-vessel definition. Its historical ending is retained, and the short continuation is distinct from the following honorific sleep term.
Guioxin is sleep expressed respectfully of an honored person. The visible short o corrects OCR y; the repeated Guio- begins the example and is physically divided from xin below.
Xin completes Guio-xin. Aru and naſaruru are alternatives for saying respectfully that the person sleeps; l is the Latin alternative marker.

Guiǒxiqi concerns form and color, Catachi, iro. The Portuguese capital is F in Figura. Enlargement shows the surviving rising arm on the right of the headword’s o; the caron reading also agrees with the subsequently consulted NINJAL headword, although the other arm is abraded.
Guiôxǒ is glossed as a carpenter, with Tacumi and tacumu printed as its Japanese explanations. The upright final S. marks written usage, and the headword’s G corrects OCR Gai-.
Guioxô pairs a fisherman with a woodcutter, Sunadori, qicori. The Portuguese first supplies fisherman and continues the second occupation below.
Homem que corta lenha gives the woodcutter half of the paired expression. It is a continuation of Guioxô, not an independent Portuguese entry.

Guioxǔ is another term for a fishing boat, Sunadorino fune. The final e of Portuguese de is almost effaced, leaving only a small stroke at letter height; de is adopted with this caveat because the trace is compatible and peſcadores completes the phrase below.

Peſcadores completes the fishing-vessel gloss and S. marks written usage. The signature and catchword printed farther right on this baseline have been separated into their own furniture zones rather than left inside the body text.
